common_name: Southport White Globe Onion (Classic American Long-Storing Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant as soon as the soil can be worked; this is a long-day heirloom that needs the extended summer daylength of northern latitudes to bulb well.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep beds weed-free and evenly watered through the bulbing period. Southport White Globe is a 19th-century American heirloom that became the standard of the old Southport, Connecticut onion-growing district, producing perfectly round, pure-white, mild-flavored bulbs with thin papery skin over crisp white flesh. It is a long-day type best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength, and while its white skin makes it more prone to sunscald and bruising in storage than yellow or red types, well-cured bulbs still keep respectably for a winter storage onion. Stop watering once tops begin to yellow and fall over, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks, and store the largest, firmest bulbs for later use.

common_name: Ebenezer Onion (Old Dutch Yellow Storage Heirloom)

planting.note: Can also be grown from sets planted as soon as the soil is workable in spring; Ebenezer is an old long-day storage onion best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free through bulb development. Ebenezer is a classic Dutch-derived heirloom onion, long grown in American gardens both from seed and from sets, producing firm, globe-to-slightly-flattened yellow-brown bulbs with pungent flesh and outstanding storage life compared to sweeter modern hybrids. It is one of the parent lines behind several later commercial yellow storage onions and remains popular with gardeners who want an old-fashioned, strong-flavored keeper for cooking rather than fresh eating. Stop watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for a few weeks, and store in a cool, dry place where it will keep considerably longer than sweet onion types.

common_name: Stockton Red Onion (California Heirloom Red Storage Onion)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil is workable; Stockton Red is an intermediate-day type adaptable to a fairly broad range of latitudes, including much of the mid-South.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and water evenly through the growing season. Stockton Red is an old California heirloom onion, named for the San Joaquin Valley growing district around Stockton, producing flattened, deep-red-skinned bulbs with pink-tinged white flesh and a flavor milder than many storage reds, making it good for both fresh eating and cooking. It is an intermediate-day type with somewhat more latitude flexibility than strict long-day heirlooms, and it stores respectably for a red onion when properly cured. Taper off watering once the tops begin to yellow and topple, then pull the bulbs, cure in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks, and store in a cool, dry spot out of direct light to preserve color and firmness.
